_README: Cell formats and cell configurations — Instrumentation spec §4. NOTE THE SPLIT: format (coin, pouch, cylindrical) is how the cell is physically built; configuration (half, full, symmetric, three-electrode) is what the measurement is ABOUT. Students routinely conflate them — a coin cell can be a half cell or a full cell. DRAFT content, review before use. Dimensions given are naming conventions only, not specifications.

formats.name: Coin cell
formats.subtitle: CR-type, e.g. CR2032
formats.summary: The standard research format: a stack of discs sealed between two metal caps. Quick to build, cheap, and reproducible enough for comparison — provided assembly is consistent.
formats.note: The CR number is a size convention, not a chemistry: in CR2032 the '20' is the diameter in mm and the '32' the height in tenths of a mm. It says nothing about what is inside.

layers.label: Positive cap
layers.detail: Forms the positive terminal and one half of the sealed casing. Also the current collector path for the positive side.

layers.label: Positive electrode
layers.detail: The positive-side active material, usually coated on a foil current collector. In a half cell against lithium this is the electrode under study.

layers.label: Separator
layers.detail: Porous membrane soaked in electrolyte. Keeps the electrodes physically apart while letting ions through. Must fully cover the electrode — an overhanging edge is what prevents an edge short.

layers.label: Negative electrode
layers.detail: The negative-side active material or, in a half cell, a lithium or sodium metal disc acting as both counter and pseudo-reference.

layers.label: Spacer disc
layers.detail: Stainless steel disc that takes up the remaining height and transmits pressure evenly. Its thickness is part of what makes assembly reproducible.

layers.label: Wave spring
layers.detail: Maintains contact pressure as the stack settles and as electrodes breathe during cycling. Inconsistent spring placement is a common source of cell-to-cell scatter.

layers.label: Gasket
layers.detail: Polymer sealing ring. Seals against electrolyte loss AND electrically insulates the two caps from each other — a gasket seated wrongly gives either a leak or a short.

layers.label: Negative cap
layers.detail: The negative terminal and the other half of the casing. Crimped onto the gasket to seal the cell.

problems: Inconsistent crimping pressure between cells, giving scatter that looks like material variation
Separator not fully covering the electrode, allowing an edge short
Too little electrolyte, so the electrode is not fully wetted
Gasket misseated — leaks, or shorts the two caps together

formats.name: Pouch cell
formats.subtitle: laminated soft-case
formats.summary: Electrode stack or wound jelly-roll sealed in a laminated aluminium foil pouch. Scales to larger capacities and shows swelling directly — which is useful information rather than only a nuisance.

layers.label: Laminate pouch
layers.detail: Aluminium-polymer laminate. Flexible, so gas generation shows as visible swelling — an early warning a rigid can hides.

layers.label: Positive tab
layers.detail: Welded external contact. Weld quality directly sets contact resistance; a poor weld looks exactly like a high-resistance electrode in the data.

layers.label: Positive electrode
layers.detail: Coated foil, often double-sided and stacked or wound with multiple layers.

layers.label: Separator
layers.detail: Between every electrode pair in the stack.

layers.label: Negative electrode
layers.detail: Usually made slightly larger than the positive electrode so its edges are not left facing bare separator.

layers.label: Negative tab
layers.detail: The negative external contact.

layers.label: Laminate pouch
layers.detail: Heat-sealed around the edges, with the tabs passing through a sealed region.

problems: Seal failure at the tab crossing, the most common leak point
Gas generation causing swelling and loss of internal contact
Uneven stack pressure across a large area
Tab weld resistance mistaken for electrode resistance

formats.name: Cylindrical cell
formats.subtitle: wound jelly-roll in a rigid can
formats.summary: Electrodes and separator wound into a spiral and sealed in a metal can. Mechanically robust and thermally well defined, but almost nothing inside can be inspected without destroying it.

layers.label: Metal can
layers.detail: Rigid casing, usually also the negative terminal. Contains internal pressure rather than deforming — so gas build-up is not visible from outside.

layers.label: Positive electrode
layers.detail: Long coated foil, wound spirally with the separator.

layers.label: Separator
layers.detail: Wound between the electrodes along the full length of the roll.

layers.label: Negative electrode
layers.detail: The counterpart foil in the winding.

layers.label: Vent / safety device
layers.detail: Pressure-relief and, in many designs, a current-interrupt device. A safety feature, not a performance one — and not something to defeat or bypass.

layers.label: Cap assembly
layers.detail: The positive terminal, insulated from the can.

problems: Internal pressure not visible from outside, unlike a pouch
Non-uniform current distribution along a long wound electrode
Thermal gradients between the core and the surface
Almost nothing can be inspected without destructive teardown

configurations.name: Half cell
configurations.measures: One electrode, against a counter that is effectively a reservoir
configurations.typical: Material under study vs Li or Na metal
configurations.formulaNote: The measured potential is dominated by the electrode under study, because the metal counter electrode's potential barely moves. It is treated as a pseudo-reference — convenient, but it is not a true reference electrode and it does polarise at higher currents.
configurations.watchFor: At high rate or over long cycling the metal electrode itself degrades, and that degradation appears in the data as though it belonged to the material under study.

configurations.name: Full cell
configurations.measures: The whole device — both electrodes together
configurations.typical: Two different insertion electrodes, as in a practical cell
configurations.formulaNote: The measured voltage is the difference between two moving potentials. You cannot attribute a feature to one electrode without a reference, because both are changing at once.
configurations.watchFor: Capacity is limited by whichever electrode runs out first, so a full-cell result reflects the pairing and the balancing, not either material alone.

configurations.name: Symmetric cell
configurations.typical: Supercapacitor devices; also diagnostic cells for isolating one interface
configurations.formulaNote: For a symmetric two-electrode device, the single-electrode-equivalent capacitance is conventionally reported as 4·I·Δt/(m_total·ΔV) — a factor of four arising from two electrodes in series each carrying half the device voltage, with m_total covering both. This is a DIFFERENT formula variant, not the same equation with different numbers.
configurations.watchFor: Comparing a symmetric-device value directly with a three-electrode single-electrode value, without converting, is one of the most common errors in supercapacitor literature.

configurations.name: Three-electrode cell
configurations.measures: One electrode, against a genuine reference, while current flows elsewhere
configurations.typical: Mechanistic studies; single-electrode behaviour inside a device
configurations.formulaNote: Because potential is measured against a stable reference carrying essentially no current, values are attributable to the single electrode under study — this is the configuration the material-level formulas assume.
configurations.watchFor: Reference placement affects how much uncompensated resistance is included, and adding a reference to a practical format such as a coin cell is difficult and can perturb what it is measuring.
